Before playing, the players tune to one another by ear, and because the tuning is not fixed the pitch can be adjusted to suit the performers. The bass strings are usually tuned only to the notes of the tonic triad, and the further from the neck a string is stopped the higher the pitch rises; the alto and soprano are mostly tuned to the natural major scale. The adungu generally does not play melodies: it outlines the harmony with single notes on the bass and tenor and triads on the soprano and alto, and then uses arpeggios to make a syncopated rhythm.

The adungu is a traditional bow harp used by the Acholi of northern Uganda and the Alur of the north-west, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.11. Its soundbox is hollowed from wood and covered with cowhide as a soundboard, and nylon strings (traditionally gut or sinew) pass through the soundboard to tuning pegs on a curved wooden frame, with six to ten strings or more being common. A small instrument is held close to the body and plucked with both hands, while a large bass instrument can be played sitting on the ground; it can be played solo, in ensemble or to accompany singing, and from the 1960s it was taken into schools as part of cultural preservation teaching.
阿杜古弓形豎琴源自烏干達北部阿喬利人與西北部阿盧爾人的傳統，屬尼羅-撒哈拉語系族: The adungu comes from the tradition of the Acholi of northern Uganda and the Alur of the north-west; it is the bow harp of Nilo-Saharan-speaking peoples and represents several centuries of musical transmission. Its name and form are also found in Teso, and the Baganda call it ennanga. During the political upheavals of the 1960s it was taken into school teaching along with other traditional instruments, as part of cultural preservation and its gradual spread through the country. Its tuning was originally pentatonic, and later, under the British presence in Uganda, it turned to the major scale of European classical music, and solo, ensemble and accompaniment forms developed.

The smaller ones are held against the body and played with both hands, while the larger bass models are played seated, the greater leverage giving a deeper, more resonant tone. The bass models are usually tuned only to the notes of the tonic triad, and the further from the neck a string is stopped the higher the pitch; the alto, tenor and soprano models can be tuned to the natural major scale. Playing is mostly not melodic, but outlines chords with arpeggios, which gives a simple harmonic progression rhythmic drive.
